concepts.title: True Story Craft as Anti-Charisma Tradition — The Cross-Batch SIGNAL (Claus / Lewis / Dicks × 2)
concepts.excerpt: Four sources from this batch — Jasper Claus (Dutch corporate-filmmaker, 17 years, NYU Film + Social Psychology master's, McKee Storynomics lineage), the Newel of Knowledge Lewis synthesis (YouTube popular-storytelling teacher), Matthew Dicks's Knowledge Project Podcast interview (58-time Moth StorySLAM champion, Storyworthy author), and Matthew Dicks's Calum Johnson Show interview (the same Dicks, different host, ~70% content overlap) — converge on a load-bearing claim across four very different storytelling contexts:

concepts.title: Charisma Is a Myth, Storytelling Is a Craft — Replace the Word (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks's central counter-position to the cultural understanding of public-speaking talent: I'd replace the word charisma with craft.

concepts.title: Story vs Anecdote (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You walk past the cotton candy machine at the state fair. The vendor hands you a paper cone of pink spun sugar that's twice the size of your head.

concepts.title: No One Wants to Hear Anything Mindset (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Most people in that room will resist the sentence at first. They have data.

concepts.title: Homework for Life — Daily Story Capture (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks has an Excel spreadsheet. Every night before he sleeps, he opens it and writes one sentence.

concepts.title: Rumination as the Locator for 5-Second Moments (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: A wedding in Maine, ten summers ago. Matt Dicks has just finished officiating.

concepts.title: Small Moments Are More Powerful Than Crazy Ones (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks has been hit by a car. Twice, actually. He's been in an armed robbery with a gun pressed to his head.

concepts.title: Storyteller Self-Centered in a Positive Way (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Most people, Matt Dicks says, feel these moments — the small interior shifts that happen during a day.

concepts.title: Five Anecdotes Always in Pocket (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks walks into a venue with five anecdotes already loaded. He doesn't know which one he'll use.

concepts.title: The 5-Second Moment of Change (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks opens the door to his son's bedroom and stands there for about four seconds.

concepts.title: And-Stories vs But-Therefore-Stories (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: A first-grader comes home from school and tells you about their day.

concepts.title: The Big Three Framework (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Calum Johnson asks Matt Dicks the question every interviewer eventually asks a master craftsman: if you had to compress everything you teach into one usable thing, what would it be?

concepts.title: Start at the End, Work Backwards (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You walk into a marketing meeting. Someone is presenting a 60-slide deck.

concepts.title: Beginning as the Opposite of the Ending — The Contrast Arc (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You walk out of The Sixth Sense into the parking lot, dazed. Bruce Willis was dead the whole time.

concepts.title: Fight for Beginnings — Half of Crafting Time (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks tells Calum Johnson something that sounds extreme until you absorb what it implies.

concepts.title: Beginnings Are Where Stories Die — The Plane-Ride Metaphor (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: The plane has taken off. You've worked for weeks on the destination — a beautiful tropical island with white sand and clear water.

concepts.title: Start With Location and Action (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks teaches fifth grade. He's been doing it for 27 years. On the first day of school every year, he teaches his ten-year-olds one specific thing about storytelling before anything else.

concepts.title: BABC Model — Start in the Middle (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks has a story he wants to tell about his son's swim test at Scout camp.

concepts.title: Time Travel Within a Story — The Default Rule (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You're telling a story. You've located the 5-second moment. You've built the scaffolding.

concepts.title: Frayed Endings, Not Knots (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Thelma & Louise ends with two women driving off a cliff holding hands.

concepts.title: Stakes, Suspense, Surprise, Humor — The Mount Rushmore (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: The point of naming exactly four is that the four are the complete set — every other engagement technique is either a sub-variant of one of these or a structural property that supports them rather than an engagement engine in itself.

concepts.title: Elephant Stakes — Grabbing Initial Attention (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Walk into a doorway and there's an elephant standing in the kitchen. You do not have to be told to notice it.

concepts.title: Backpacks — Share Your Plan, Then Derail It (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You're in the audience. The storyteller tells you he's been chasing a 10-year-old for 18 minutes and can't catch him.

concepts.title: Breadcrumbs — Subtle Foreshadowing Clues (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You're in the audience for the spoon-of-power story. Matt Dicks is in the middle of describing his fifth-grade class.

concepts.title: Hourglasses — Stretching the Reveal (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks is approaching the climax of the spoon-of-power story. Jamie is about to walk over to him and place the spoon around his neck for the first time.

concepts.title: Crystal Balls — Out-Loud Predictions (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Dallas Cowboys fans don't wait until Monday morning to find out if their team won.

concepts.title: Camo Bombs — Detail Planting for Late Explosion (Lewis)
concepts.excerpt: Lewis is telling a story about a night in Slovenia in 2018. He's at a hostel.

concepts.title: Suspense as Strategic Exclusion and Inclusion (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You sit down with the Sunday crossword. You read the clue: five-letter word for the color blue.

concepts.title: The Cinematographer Metaphor — Narrow to Wide Lens (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks tells storytellers to be cinematographers with their words.

concepts.title: Four Tools for Painting Over Boring Parts — Humor, Suspense, Novelty, Never-Done-Before (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: On Saturday Night Live, Andy Kaufman walks onto the stage carrying a record player.

concepts.title: Leverage Audience Imagination — Don't Describe (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks drops a bowl of blueberries on the kitchen floor in one of his stories.

concepts.title: Not-Description Is More Powerful Than Description (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matt Dicks asks Shane Parrish, mid-interview, to feel a small thing. If I say "Shane is smart," that's fine.

concepts.title: Add Location to Every Scene — Cinema in the Mind (Lewis)
concepts.excerpt: The principle is Lewis's named extension of the Dicks location-and-action rule.

concepts.title: Humor Changes Brain Chemistry in Storytelling (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: The claim is consequential. Most amateur storytellers treat humor as decoration — make it funny when you can, but the real work is the content.

concepts.title: Laugh in the First 30 Seconds — Three Effects (Dicks / Lewis)
concepts.excerpt: Lewis names the effect more precisely in his masterclass: Make the audience laugh within the first 30 seconds of you opening your mouth telling the story, because this does three things really key things.

concepts.title: Laugh-Laugh-Laugh-Cry — The Date-Then-Dump Mechanic (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You've been dating someone for three months. You've decided they're a monster.

concepts.title: Milk Cans and Baseballs — Humor Technique #1 (Lewis)
concepts.excerpt: You go to the carnival. There's a booth with milk cans stacked in a pyramid.

concepts.title: Babies and Blenders — Incongruity Humor (Lewis)
concepts.excerpt: The mechanic is incongruity-engineered laughter. Pair two concepts that violate audience-expectation about what belongs together.

concepts.title: Specificity Is Funny (Lewis)
concepts.excerpt: I'm pouring milk over a bowl of brown flakes. I'm pouring milk over a bowl of cereal.

concepts.title: End with Heart, Not Joke — The Vulnerability Landing (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You finish your story. There is a moment of silence in the room. Nobody laughs.

concepts.title: Vulnerability Receives Extraordinary Response — The Wall That Does Not Exist (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You are about to tell, on stage or at a dinner table, the thing you have been keeping quiet for years.

concepts.title: The Game Played with the Audience — Remember, Don't Memorize (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: There's a game running every time someone tells a story to an audience.

concepts.title: Speaking To, Not At — The Conversational Shift (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks is backstage at the Brooklyn Historical Society. He is about to give a talk to a substantial audience.

concepts.title: Talk to Individuals, Not the Group — The Three-People Tactic (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You are on stage. The audience is two hundred faces. The temptation — universal among speakers — is to address the audience as a unit, scanning across the room in even sweeps, eye contact landing on no one in particular.

concepts.title: Nervousness as Connector — Disclosed Anxiety as the Highest-Leverage Opening (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: A best man stands up at a wedding reception. He has the microphone. The room is two hundred people, half of whom he does not know.

concepts.title: Imperfection Is the Beauty — The Burns Maxim (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You are on stage. You are telling the story of the day your mother called to tell you the diagnosis.

concepts.title: The Power-Out Test — If the Lights Cut, Will Anyone Care? (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks tells two anecdotes about being in movie theaters where the power went out mid-film.

concepts.title: Audience Is Happy I'm Still Talking — The Platonic Ideal (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You are eight minutes into a story. The story has nine more minutes to go.

concepts.title: Four-Anchor Memorization — The Skeleton You Hold, the Flesh You Improvise (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: The amateur storyteller's instinct, faced with a stage appearance, is to memorize the whole story word for word.

concepts.title: The Cardinal Sins of Storytelling — The Composite Anti-Rules (Dicks Tradition)
concepts.excerpt: You finish a story. Before you take it to the stage, you owe the story one last pass — an audit not against what it is doing, but against what it must not be doing.

concepts.title: Truth in Stories — You Can Edit, You Cannot Lie (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Two cuts the storyteller is allowed to make: combine three friends into one character because the story does not need three; compress a six-week saga into a three-day weekend because the runtime does not permit six weeks.

concepts.title: You Own Everything That Happened to You — The Lamott Maxim (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You are about to tell a story that includes your father, and your father did something in the story that does not show him well.

concepts.title: Strategic Listening — The Storyteller's Meta-Skill (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You and your spouse are in a movie theater watching Wonder Woman. Your spouse is leaning forward, gripping the armrest during the No Man's Land scene, eyes wide when Diana crests the trench.

concepts.title: Structure Trumps Sentences — The Dena Principle (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: At the Moth StorySLAM in New York, a woman named Dena takes the stage.

concepts.title: One Camera True Storytelling Method — Story + Insight + Message + Logo (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Jasper Claus's corporate-filmmaking shop, One Camera (Amsterdam, 17 years of practice, 5,000+ films for Heineken, Unilever, Coca-Cola, Microsoft, FrieslandCampina, others), has developed an operational framework for how corporate films should be structured.

concepts.title: The Three Pitfalls of Corporate Storytelling — The Named Failure Catalog (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Jasper Claus's seventeen years of corporate-filmmaking practice (5,000+ films for Heineken, Unilever, Coca-Cola, Microsoft, and other large multinational clients) has surfaced three reliable failure-patterns that destroy corporate storytelling projects before they have a chance to succeed.

concepts.title: Negaphobia — Fear of Narrative Darkness (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: The most beautiful thing we have to offer to our audiences is the hope and warmth of a feel-good ending, like Cupid's arrow shot straight through the heart.

concepts.title: The Bathtub Story Graph — Three-Level Struggle Architecture (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Jasper Claus's One Camera shop developed its own story-arc diagram across years of corporate-film practice.

concepts.title: Universal Value and Its Upside-Down — The Story-Engine Pair (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Within Jasper Claus's True Storytelling Method, the story-development process begins with identifying the universal human value that the message-and-insight combination implies — and then identifying that value's upside-down version.

concepts.title: The Main Character Is Not Your Brand — The Identification Rule (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: The principle is operational and resists corporate-client preference. Most corporate clients want their brand to be the main character — the brand is, after all, what the film is for.

concepts.title: The 90/10 Story-Message Screen-Time Ratio (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Jasper Claus's operational screen-time ratio for corporate-films: 90% of screen time should be the story; 10% should be the message.

concepts.title: Remixing the Story Graph — Flashbacks, Flash-Forwards, Omissions (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: The bathtub story graph has ten sections in classical sequence.

concepts.title: Insight as Bridge Between Message and Story — The Universal-Truth Anchor (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Two cognitive contents need to meet in a corporate film. The first is the message — what the sender wants the audience to think or feel about the sender's organization.

concepts.title: Touch the Heart and the Mind Will Open — The McKee Maxim (Claus / McKee)
concepts.excerpt: Jasper Claus's corporate-filmmaking practice is built around the maxim.

concepts.title: Reunion and Redemption — The Two Kama-Muta-Producing Archetypes (Claus / Fiske)
concepts.excerpt: Two narrative archetypes reliably produce kama muta in audiences. Anthropologist Alan Fiske's cross-cultural research documents both as having consistent triggers and consistent affective consequences.

concepts.title: Research as Cliche Prevention — The Discipline Beneath the Craft (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Jasper Claus's central craft-discipline insight: truth is found in reality.

concepts.title: Three Qualifying Questions — The Pre-Project Diagnostic (Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Question 1. Are you aware that in a storytelling film you will not be able to include a lot of information?

concepts.title: Theme-Meaning-Message Content Match — Let the Story Carry the Pitch (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: A scientist named John needs to communicate the company message: our apple-extract delivery tube saves lives.

concepts.title: Stories Create Markers in Audience Lives — The Echo Through Decades (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: A storyteller delivers a story you have not heard before. Three minutes in, a specific line lands — something about a grandfather standing at a window watching the sun come up the morning his wife died.

concepts.title: Outrageous Secrets as Sales Signal — The Counterintuitive Tell (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You are in a sales meeting. The prospect is a senior executive at a mid-sized company.

concepts.title: First-Last-Best-Worst — The Four-Prompt Improvisation Game (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: The Dicks storytelling drill: pick any category of life experience that has multiple instances (kisses, jobs, road trips, fights with siblings, conversations with strangers, embarrassing moments at parties).

concepts.title: Keynote as Six Stories, Not One Story (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You've been asked to deliver a keynote. 60-90 minutes. You decide to tell a story.

concepts.title: Movie Openings Predict Endings — The Pattern Across Films (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: When Harry Met Sally opens with an elderly couple sitting on a couch, telling the camera how they met.

concepts.title: Independence Day — The Disrespect-to-Respect Engine Hidden Under the Disaster Movie (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Independence Day (1996) is a summer-blockbuster alien-invasion film. Aliens arrive; aliens destroy major cities; humans counter-attack; humans defeat the aliens through a computer-virus trick.

concepts.title: Writing and Telling Are Different Arts — Why Sedaris Reads Flat on Stage (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: David Sedaris is one of the most celebrated American essayists alive.

concepts.title: Punch Sentences Get Their Own Paragraph — Writing the Vocal Pause (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: You are watching a comedy on streaming TV with the closed captions on.

concepts.title: Against the Topic Sentence — Why School Writing Kills Storytelling (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks collaborated with a sociologist on a writing project. The two of them were working on a book that would combine the sociologist's research findings with Dicks's storytelling craft.

concepts.title: Read Aloud Six Times for Every One Time You Edit — Teaching Kids to Write (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks's daughter wrote a novel as a child. Not a polished novel — a child's novel, full of the inconsistencies and improvisations and abandoned subplots that children's novels contain.

concepts.title: Evolutionary Storytelling — Survival and Navigation Mechanism (Dicks / Claus)
concepts.excerpt: Why do humans tell stories at all? Why is the storytelling impulse near-universal across cultures, time periods, and developmental ages?

concepts.title: Kama Muta — Being Moved by Love (Claus / Fiske)
concepts.excerpt: You are watching a film. A grandfather, separated from his grandson by a misunderstanding that lasted twenty years, walks back into the boy's kitchen.

concepts.title: Storytelling as Being Truly Known — The Deeper Function Beneath the Craft (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks's framing of why storytelling matters beyond the craft and beyond the audience-response: storytelling is the mechanism by which we become truly known by others.

concepts.title: Inattention as Storyteller Origin — The Childhood Engine Beneath the Adult Craft (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: Matthew Dicks's autobiographical observation about his own origins as a storyteller: I was a child nobody listened to.

concepts.title: Marginalized Voices Lack Story-Space, Not Stories — Reframing What's Actually Missing (Dicks)
concepts.excerpt: The common framing of voice-marginalization in cultural discourse: certain groups lack voice.
